newsitem.title: UK: Rally by gold struggles at $350 barrier.
newsitem.headline: Rally by gold struggles at $350 barrier.

text.p: Gold struggled to break above the threshold of $350 an ounce in a strong rally on Monday while prices for platinum and palladium also advanced, despite news that Russia may be near to resuming delayed exports.
Gold was fixed on Monday afternoon in London unchanged from the morning at $348.20 an ounce.
But gains in New York Comex gold futures later gave the market another kick to challenge $350, a one-month high, with gains totalling $7.50 from Friday.
The fall in the dollar against the yen to a four-year low of 118 shifted interest from currencies into gold.
Platinum was indicated at $398.05/$399.05 an ounce, its highest since February 28 and $12.05 up on the day. Palladium set a fresh two-year high of $175.65, up $10.15.
Both rose after a knee jerk downward reaction to a news that a Russian official had said a decree allowing resumed shipments to key importer Japan had been signed.
The forward market remained gripped by a liquidity squeeze, dealers explained.
"I don't think it will have a long lasting effect, just simply putting to right situations of physical agreement between Japan and Russia," said one.

He said there were concerns that Russian stockpiles might be less than initially thought and added, "I don't think we're going to see a huge correction on the downside, not unless the liquidity returns to normal."
One-month lease rates for palladium were quoted at a substantial 25 percent. Platinum was lent at 14 percent.

Vladimir Rykbin, head of the precious metals department at the Russian Finance Ministry, said the export decree "has definitely been signed" but that he did not know when long-delayed talks with Japanese buyers would resume.
Analysts said once 1997 contracts were negotiated with key buyer Japan prices would ease, but not dramatically.
"It is possible that huge amount of fund interest in the market these days will keep palladium prices in the $150-$155 an ounce area," said Ted Arnold, metals analyst at Merrill Lynch.
Gold at close to $350 an ounce was approaching territory in which producers may release pent-up sales, analysts said.
A trader recalled that much recent selling in gold had been psychological, in anticipation of central bank sales.
"After the depressing mood earlier this year, it will take a lot of interest to get back up to the $360s," said the dealer.
